name: EFR32ZG23B020F512IM48-B
title: Sub-GHz Z-Wave wireless SoC, Cortex-M33 at 78 MHz, 512 kB flash, 64 kB RAM, up to +20 dBm
summary: The EFR32ZG23 family puts a 78 MHz Cortex-M33 with FPU and TrustZone, 512 kB of flash, 64 kB of RAM and a sub-GHz transceiver for Z-Wave, Z-Wave Long Range, Sidewalk and proprietary links on one die, with a +14 dBm or +20 dBm PA and a Secure Vault security engine (Mid or High). It runs from one 1.71 V to 3.8 V supply, optionally through its own buck converter, and sleeps at about 1.5 µA in EM2 with all RAM kept. The EFR32ZG23B020F512IM48 is the QFN48 member with the 20 dBm PA, Secure Vault High, an LCD driver, 31 GPIO and a -40 °C to +125 °C rating.
key_figures: 4.0 mA at 916 MHz 100 kbps GFSK, 3.3 V with DC-DC
25.0 mA at +14 dBm, 85.5 mA at +20 dBm, 916 MHz
1.5 µA, 64 kB RAM kept, RTC on LFXO
12 bits at 1 Msps, 16 bits at 76.9 ksps

notes: Code: EFR32ZG23, then the Secure Vault level (A Mid, B High), three feature digits (first unused; second 1 = 14 dBm PA, 2 = 20 dBm PA; third 1 = high-quality HFCLKOUT pin), F for flash, the flash size in kB, the temperature grade (G -40 to +85 °C, I -40 to +125 °C), M for QFN, the pin count, the revision letter, and an optional R for tape and reel.

Top marking: FFFF family code (F or Z, G, series 2, configuration 3); PPPPPP option code (security A or B, three feature codes, flash H = 512k, G = 256k, F = 128k, temperature grade G or I); TTTTTT trace code whose first letter is the die revision; YY assembly year; WW assembly week.

operation.text: A Cortex-M33 application core with DSP extensions, FPU, TrustZone and ETM sits beside a sub-GHz radio subsystem that has its own Cortex-M0+ controller, frequency synthesiser, modem, frame controller and buffer controller. A separate secure engine with its own CPU runs Secure Vault. The application core reaches 1.50 Dhrystone MIPS/MHz and is debugged over 2-pin Serial Wire.

There are two RF paths. RF0 uses SUBG_I0 into one LNA and SUBG_O0 from the PA; RF1 uses SUBG_I1 and SUBG_O1. On-chip switches pick which output is active. The PA is a +14 dBm or +20 dBm block, depending on the ordering code.

A fractional-N synthesiser makes the LO for the receive mixer and modulates the carrier directly when transmitting. Its resolution is better than 24.8 Hz and it settles fast, so the radio wakes quickly. It covers 110 MHz to 970 MHz in five ranges.

Low-IF design: LNA, I/Q mixer, filtering and an IF ADC, with demodulation done digitally. The IF is set between 150 kHz and 1371 kHz, with high- or low-side injection to dodge an image interferer. Receive bandwidth runs from 0.1 kHz to 2530 kHz. AGC guards against saturation, and the radio can be calibrated for its band on request. Block and convolutional FEC and DSSS are supported. RSSI is captured per frame and can be read live for proximity, CA or LBT. Antenna diversity drives an external switch with complementary outputs.

Direct conversion: for constant-envelope formats the modulator steers the synthesiser's phase and frequency. A configurable shaping filter (Gaussian or raised cosine, any BT) can shape symbols or chips. CSMA-CA and LBT timing can be handled by the hardware. Modulations: 2/4 (G)FSK, O-QPSK DSSS, (G)MSK and OOK.

The radio controller times receiver and transmitter enable, runs calibration and handles frame timing including LBT and CSMA-CA. The buffer controller manages up to four RAM buffers, each 64 to 4096 bytes and usable for RX, TX or both, so data is not copied. A trace unit can stream TX data, RX data and state over a one-pin UART or two-pin SPI output at a chosen rate.

For duty-cycled receivers, preamble sense mode detects a preamble quickly to cut average receive current. It works with 2(G)FSK only and gains most with long preambles and low data rates; it is reached through the signal qualifier.

Up to 31 pins, each input or output with open-drain, open-source and glitch filtering options, routed to peripherals and to the PRS, with asynchronous interrupts. Ports A and B work in EM2/EM3 for low-energy peripherals and as wake-up pins; ports C and D keep their state through EM2 and hand back to peripherals on exit. A few pins wake the part from EM4 (EM4WUx in the alternate function table).
Scans a matrix of up to 6 × 8 keys with its own debounce and settling timing, autonomously in EM0 and EM1, interrupting on a press; a key press can wake the part from as deep as EM3.

HFXO: 39.0 MHz crystal with built-in, finely tunable load capacitors, or an external clock such as a TCXO. LFXO: 32.768 kHz crystal. HFRCO: 1 MHz to 80 MHz with fast start. FSRCO: fixed 20 MHz. LFRCO: 32.768 kHz. ULFRCO: 1 kHz for the lowest-power timing. The CMU gates each peripheral clock individually.

TIMER0 is 32-bit and TIMER1 to TIMER4 are 16-bit, each with three capture/compare/PWM channels and dead-time insertion. LETIMER0 is a 24-bit timer that keeps running down to EM3 and can generate waveforms. SYSRTC is a 32-bit counter running to EM3; BURTC is a 32-bit counter running in every mode including EM4; both wake the system at set intervals. Two watchdogs offer windowed monitoring and can watch PRS-driven activity.

USART0 does UART with flow control, RS-485, SPI, MicroWire, 3-wire, ISO7816, IrDA and I2S. EUSART0 to EUSART2 do UART, RS-485, IrDA and high-speed SPI with buffering in EM0/EM1. On ports A or B, EUSART0 also works in EM2: UART up to 9600 baud from a 32.768 kHz clock, or as an SPI secondary in EM2/EM3 that wakes the system on received data. Two I2C blocks cover 10 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s (standard, fast, fast-plus) as main or secondary with SMBus arbitration and timeouts and address matching in low-energy modes; I2C0 works to EM3, I2C1 to EM1.

The 12-channel PRS links producer peripherals to consumers with edge detection and AND/OR/NOT logic, without the CPU. LESENSE drives up to 16 sensors through the comparators, ADC and DAC, with a state machine that processes results without the CPU, and runs in EM2 as well as EM0/EM1; it handles LC, resistive and capacitive sensors.

A dedicated secure engine keeps cryptographic keys and operations away from the M33. Both levels have a TRNG, secure boot from ROM (RTSL), secure debug lock/unlock with public-key authenticated unlock, and DPA countermeasures on the AES and ECC engines. High adds anti-tamper, secure attestation and PUF-based key management. The accelerator handles AES-128/192/256 (ECB, CTR, CBC, CFB, GCM, CCM, CBC-MAC, GMAC), ChaCha20, ECDH and ECDSA on P-192 to P-521, Curve25519 and Ed25519, ECJ-PAKE, PBKDF2, SHA-1, SHA-2 up to 512 and Poly1305.

RTSL checks a chain of firmware starting from immutable ROM, blocking rollback and unsigned code, including over-the-air updates. The TRNG draws entropy from thermal noise, runs the start-up tests of NIST SP800-90B and AIS-31 and the online tests of SP800-90C, and is meant to seed a deterministic generator.

On Secure Vault High parts, keys are wrapped with a key derived at each power-up from a PUF seed; that key is seen only by the AES engine and vanishes at power-down, so any number of wrapped keys can be stored, even off-chip. Internal tamper sensing watches voltage, temperature, EM pulses and the secure subsystem, and 8 tamper pins take external sources such as case switches. Each event can raise an interrupt, a reset or erase the PUF data, making keys unrecoverable; a counter with threshold and refresh period filters false alarms. Each part also holds its own key pair, made in production, with an X.509 certificate chained to the Silicon Labs CA stored in OTP, so it can prove it is genuine by signing a challenge.

A hybrid SAR and delta-sigma converter: 12 bits at 1 Msps, 16 bits at up to 76.9 ksps, with hardware oversampling, internal references and single-ended or differential inputs from many sources. Differential pairs use even pins for positive and odd pins for negative.

Two comparators with programmable speed against current, two 6-bit reference dividers, and supply monitoring with an interrupt on crossing a threshold. The VDAC is a fully differential 12-bit 500 ksps converter with two channels that works down to EM3 and can play waveforms through DMA and a timer. The die temperature sensor reads to about ± 2 °C after software linearisation.

On the QFN48 parts the LCD driver runs up to 4 × 20 segments, with a boost that lifts the LCD voltage above the supply, a charge-redistribution scheme that cuts LCD current by up to 40 %, animation without the CPU and a frame-counter wake-up; it keeps running in EM2.

EM0 active, EM1 sleep, EM2 deep sleep, EM3 stop, EM4 shutoff. The EMU switches between them, powers down unused RAM blocks and scales the core LDO (which feeds DECOUPLE): VSCALE2 allows full speed, VSCALE1 up to 40 MHz in EM0/EM1, and VSCALE0 saves more in EM2/EM3. The EMU changes the level itself on mode transitions; while it scales in EM0 the CPU halts and RAM is unavailable.

PDHV is always on, down to EM4. PD0A is the EM2/EM3 base domain and stays on in EM0 to EM3. PD0B, PD0C and PD0D power further EM2/EM3 peripherals only when one of them is enabled, and switching any of them on also brings up PD0E. PD1 holds the CPU and EM0/EM1 peripherals and is off in EM2, EM3 and EM4. Each PD0 sub-domain adds its own current in EM2/EM3.

The buck converter needs one inductor (2.2 µH) and one capacitor (4.7 µF) and stays efficient from EM0 to EM3. It takes VREGVDD in and produces DVDD at 1.8 V; it needs VREGVDD of at least 2.2 V to regulate at full load. RF noise mitigation lets it run without much loss of sensitivity. A supply monitor (2.0 V to 2.3 V, 0.1 V steps) can interrupt software so the converter is switched to bypass at low supply. Soft switching at boot and on regulate-to-bypass changes limits slew and inrush. When it is not used, DVDD must be tied to VREGVDD on the board.

With the DC-DC, DVDD is its output and must not be driven from outside, and VREGVDD must be at least DVDD. Without it, DVDD and VREGVDD are one net. AVDD and IOVDD are independent of each other and of the rest, though leakage can rise if DVDD is unpowered while they are up. DVDD must be at least DECOUPLE, and PAVDD at least RFVDD.

Reset sources include the supply monitors, the RESETn pin, software, core lockup and the watchdogs. RESETn has a 44 kΩ typical pull-up to DVDD and must be held low for at least 100 ns. DVDD is watched by the DVDD BOD in EM0/EM1 and by a slower LE DVDD BOD in EM2 to EM4; AVDD and IOVDD have their own BODs in every mode.

Flash is read and written by the M33 and the LDMA in EM0 and EM1. An information block holds user data and lock bits, plus a read-only page of calibration data. Flash keeps data 10 years and endures 10,000 erase cycles. The LDMA links and stages transfers without software.
From reset to application takes about 34 ms with secure-boot checks off and no bootloader, rising to about 65 ms with application and second-stage bootloader checks on a 350 kB image.

Each band uses a discrete network between SUBG_O/SUBG_I and a 50 Ω antenna: one for 868/915/920 MHz up to +14 dBm, one for +20 dBm, and one for 433 MHz. Exact parts (tolerance, size, maker) follow the development board bill of materials. Further system connections are covered in application note AN0002.2.

Land patterns follow IPC-7351. The stencil is laser-cut, electro-polished stainless steel 0.101 mm thick with trapezoidal walls, perimeter apertures 1:1 with the pads. The centre pad takes a 3 × 3 array of openings: 0.90 mm squares at 1.20 mm pitch on QFN40, 1.10 mm squares at 1.30 mm pitch on QFN48. QFN48 pads are non-solder-mask-defined with at least 60 µm mask clearance. No-clean type-3 paste and a J-STD-020 reflow profile are recommended.
